title: Brendan Eich's Ten-Day Sprint and Why JavaScript 'Looks Like Java' (1995)
explainer: In May 1995, Netscape engineer Brendan Eich prototyped the entire first version of JavaScript (then code-named 'Mocha') in ten contiguous days, under pressure to ship something before Netscape's partnership announcement with Sun. Management required the syntax to superficially resemble Java for marketing reasons even though Eich designed the underlying object model to be prototype-based rather than class-based - which is exactly why JavaScript's curly-brace syntax looks Java-like while its object system behaves completely differently.

title: Why JavaScript Is Also Called ECMAScript (1997)
explainer: Once Microsoft shipped its own compatible-but-divergent JScript, Netscape handed JavaScript's specification to the European standards body Ecma International in late 1996 so that competing vendors could agree on one shared language rather than fragmenting the web into incompatible dialects. The result, ratified in June 1997 as ECMA-262, is why the formal language standard is named 'ECMAScript' even though almost everyone just calls it JavaScript in practice.
